title: Balance and Swap
big_idea: Adjust one side, adjust the other
child_idea: An equals sign means both sides are the same amount, like a balanced see-saw. If one number goes up, another goes down by the same amount to keep the balance.

spine.reason: Children move real small things between two plates and see what stays equal.

topics: The equals sign as 'is the same amount as' (signs + - =)
A missing number in a number sentence (blanks only, no letters)
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. It is not a claim that the program covers the school syllabus, and it must not appear on child or parent pages as 'MOE-aligned'. Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose: this lesson uses two-digit sums, tens and give-and-take, which the class explores with plates, tens bars and a worked partner step before anyone writes. The equals sign as balance is Primary 1. Compensation (giving and taking between two addends, as in 49 + 26 = 50 + 25) is beyond Primary 1 and sits at Think harder only. Letters for unknowns are Primary 6, so the lesson uses blanks only. The owner or a tutor should confirm that compensation placement.

contest_moves: balance both sides of the equals sign
give and take (compensation) between two addends
say two sums are equal without adding
three numbers, four true number sentences: the whole and its two parts (T5)
objectives: Say that = means 'is the same amount as' and check whether two sums balance.
Find the missing number in a sentence such as 6 + 3 = 5 + ___ by thinking about how the numbers moved, not only by adding.
Know give and take: when one number goes up, the other goes down by the same amount and the total stays the same.
Use give and take to decide that two sums are equal without adding (Think harder), and to make an addition easier (49 + 26 = 50 + 25).

remember: Bonds to 20 (how many more make 20, from 11 to 19)
What = means: the same amount on both sides
joining_cold.assumes: Counting in tens to 100, pairs that make 10, and adding and taking away small numbers within 10 with fingers or objects. Nothing from the earlier Term 1 lessons is needed: the warm-up re-teaches bonds to 10 and 20 and the meaning of =, and the sums that follow use two plates and small things first. No carrying is ever needed.
holiday_topics_revisited: Number bonds to 10 and 20 (Number Bond Inquiry)
joining_cold.note: Not one of the lessons hardest to miss in Term 1 (Lessons 1 and 5 to 7 are), and Lessons 9 and 10 do not depend on it. A make-up is still recommended because Term 2 Lesson 3 (Picture Equations) builds on balance. The safest lesson to skip in Term 1 is Lesson 4. A child who misses this one watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2. The tens-only questions S5 and S7 are easier after Lesson 6 (jumps of ten); the kit tens bars may be used.

child: About 30 small things of one kind: buttons, dried pasta, paper clips or coins of one kind
Two plates, bowls or sheets of paper (one marked LEFT and one marked RIGHT)
The printed workbook (pages 1 to 5) and the kit page (tens bars and ones squares), already cut out by a grown-up
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
tutor: A slide deck, and two plates with about 20 small things to show on camera if you wish
A visible clock or a timer on your own device (the deck has no timer slide)
kit_pages: Tens bars (9) and ones squares (20), printed on page 6 of the workbook: the same kit page as Lesson 1. In this lesson they are an optional help for the two-digit sums; cut them out before the lesson.
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought: everything can be found at home. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Small things never go near the mouth or ears.

timing.notes: A 2-minute opening (the routine was taught in Lesson 1 and is said again in one line), so Explore gets 16 minutes for hands-on balancing. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer; the optional Go further slide is used only if the lesson is on time.
skip_order: In a slow class the workbook runs about 3 minutes over: take it from the 5-minute flex buffer and shorten choice time, not the exit ticket
optional items and extra quick questions first
then any quick-fire in the mini-lesson

sneak_peek.q1: Ravi has 6 red beads and 4 blue beads. Siti has 5 red beads and 5 blue beads. Do they have the same number of beads? Draw dots to help, then circle Yes or No.
sneak_peek.q2: 8 + 5 = 9 + ___. What number goes in the blank? Write how you know.
sneak_peek.a2: 4. 9 is 1 more than 8, so the blank is 1 less than 5. (Both sides make 13.)

opening.say: If you are watching the recording: hello! Get a pencil, paper, two plates and your small things. Pause or rewind any time.
opening.action: Gather your workbook, pencil, paper, two plates and small things. Press play when ready.

remember.say: Recording: join in! Show your fingers and say each answer out loud. Pause if you need longer.
remember.action: Play along. Show and say each answer before the video does.

sneak.say: Recording: pause now and try both puzzles on your paper. Guessing is fine. Press play for the next part.
sneak.action: Pause. Try both puzzles on your own paper. A guess is fine.

explore.say: Recording: pause now. Put your small things on the two plates and try each balance. Press play when you have tried.
explore.action: Pause. Build each balance on your two plates. Write what you find.

mini.say: Recording: keep watching and copy the examples. Rewind if you miss a step.
mini.action: Watch and copy the examples. Rewind any step you missed.

break.say: Recording: stand up and join in! Arms out wide like a see-saw.
break.action: Stand up. Arms out like a see-saw and show the fingers.

work.say: Recording: pause now and do workbook page 1. When you finish a page, press play to check it.
work.action: Pause. Do page 1, then play to check. Then page 2. Then choose a page to try.

talk.say: Recording: pause. Tell a grown-up your answer to the talk question, and say why.
talk.action: Pause. Explain your answer to someone at home, with a reason.

exit.say: Recording: pause and do the exit ticket on your own. Then press play to check it.
exit.action: Pause. Do the exit ticket alone, then play to check it.

look.say: Recording: pause and fill in your look-back box. You can pass.
look.action: Pause. Fill in the look-back box, or pass.

flex.say: Recording: well done for finishing! Show a grown-up one thing you found out.
flex.action: Show a grown-up your workbook and tell them one thing you found out.

lines.text: Greet the whole group warmly, before the recording starts. Check that you can see each child, or ask the grown-up.
Hello, inquirers! Pencil ready, two plates and your small things on the table. Cameras can be on or off, as you like.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. You may keep your microphone and camera off.
Start the recording now. Do not use children's first names on the recording.
@rec
Microphone off until I ask you to speak. To answer, say it with me on three, show fingers, or give a thumbs up. Nobody holds paper up to the camera.
Today is about balance, like a see-saw. A see-saw is level when both sides hold the same. Numbers can balance too. Let us find out how.
Greet the whole group warmly. Do not use children's first names on the recording.

Keep this to two minutes. Say the recording statement and the microphone routine in the same words every lesson, for anyone who joined late. The inquirer rules were taught in Lesson 1; a child who is new may hear them in one sentence: notice it, test it, explain why, mistakes help us.
@rec
Today's tool is Act it out. Use counters, paper or people to show it.
Point at the tool on page 1 of the workbook.
Fingers to ten. I say a number. Show me how many more fingers make ten.
Seven. How many more to make ten?
Four?
Nine?
Six?
Two?
Now to twenty. Look at the full ten-frame and the extra counters. Thirteen is ten and three.
Thirteen. How many more make twenty?
Sixteen?
Eighteen?
Fifteen?
If a child hesitates on 16: point to the 6, ask how many more make ten (4), and say the other ten is already there.
Now the equals sign. It does not mean the answer comes next. It means: is the same amount as. Three plus four is the same amount as five plus two.
Is three plus four the same amount as five plus two? Thumbs up or down.
Is three plus four the same amount as six plus two?
Is four plus four the same amount as five plus three?

Answers: 3, 6, 1, 4, 8 then 7, 4, 2, 5 then yes (7 and 7), no (7 and 8), yes (8 and 8). Children answer with fingers, thumbs or a whispered number. Nobody writes. A child new to bonds sees the ten-frame first, then says the number.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Ravi has 6 red beads and 4 blue beads. Siti has 5 red beads and 5 blue beads. Do they have the same number of beads? Draw dots to help, then circle Yes or No.
Children draw dots or count and write yes or no.
Puzzle two. 8 plus 5 equals 9 plus a blank. What number goes in the blank? Write how you know.
Children write or draw their answer.
Thank you. Keep your paper and your own answer: nobody shows it. We will come back to puzzle two later, and you can check your own thinking then.

Puzzle 1 answer: yes, 10 each. Puzzle 2 answer: 4. Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who drew the two sides, or who said 9 is one more so the blank is one less). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today your hands are the teachers. Put your two plates side by side: left and right. On the left plate make a pile of six and a pile of four. Count them all.
On the right plate make a pile of five. Now make a second pile on the right plate so that both plates hold the same. How many are in your second pile?
Round 1a: children build and count, and show a thumbs up when the plates match.
How many in the second pile? How do you know the plates match?
Again. Left plate: seven and three. Right plate: eight and a second pile. Find the second pile.
Round 1b: children build. Answer 2.
One more. Left plate: nine and two. Right plate: eight and a second pile.
Round 1c: children build. Answer 3.
Round two: give and take. Left pile seven, right pile five. Count all the things on both piles. Now take one thing from the seven and give it to the five. Count all the things again.
Children build 7 and 5, count 12, move one across (6 and 6), count again.
Seven and five became six and six. Did the total change?
Do it again. Give one more across: five and seven. Again: four and eight. Count the total each time.
Children give one across twice more and count the total each time.
Now start again with seven and five. Give three across. What do you get? Count the total.
Children try giving 3 across from 7 and 5 (4 and 8). The total is still 12.
Round three. Left plate: eight and four. Right plate: nine and a second pile. The nine is one more than the eight. So what must the second pile be?
Children build and test. Answer 3.
One more. Left: six and five. Right: eight and a second pile. Eight is two more than six.
Children build and test. Answer 3.
What did you notice? When a number on one side got greater, what happened to the other number?
When one number goes up, the other goes down by the same amount. That keeps the balance. We call it give and take.
A child who changes both piles the same way (7 and 5 to 8 and 6): ask them to count all; is it still the same as before? Then take one back from the second pile.
A child with too few things: use the kit bars and squares, or fewer things: 6 and 4 against 5 and 5 is enough.
Main room only: no breakout rooms in this lesson. Building with the plates is for every child; the what-if card on the first explore slide is for any child who wants it, and nobody is named.
@rec
Look. Five plus three on the left. Four plus four on the right. Both sides make eight. So the two sides balance, and we write an equals sign between them.
What does the equals sign mean?
Here is give and take. Seven plus five is twelve. I take one from the seven, so it is six. I give that one to the five, so it is six. Six plus six. Still twelve.
If I take one from the seven, what must I do to the five?
Your turn. Write the missing number on your paper: 8 plus 6 equals 7 plus a blank. 9 plus 4 equals 10 plus a blank. 6 plus 5 equals 4 plus a blank.
Children write three numbers. Wait until most have stopped writing.
Seven. Three. Seven.
Now bigger numbers. Twenty-five plus eighteen equals twenty-seven plus a blank. I do not need to add yet. The twenty-five became twenty-seven: two more. So the eighteen must go down by two.
What number is two less than eighteen?
Sixteen. Let us check. Twenty-five plus eighteen is forty-three. Twenty-seven plus sixteen is forty-three. It balances.
Last idea. Are forty-seven plus eighteen and forty-five plus twenty the same? Do not add. Look at how the numbers moved.
Forty-seven went to forty-five. What happened to eighteen? Same total or different?

The 2 moved from one number to the other. So the totals are the same. Now look at the right side of the slide: twenty-nine plus fourteen and thirty plus fifteen. Both numbers went up, so the total went up.
Quick-fire. Is it balanced? Do not add. Look at how the numbers moved. Thumbs up for balanced, thumbs down for not.
Six plus five equals seven plus four?
Eight plus three equals nine plus three?
Twenty plus fourteen equals twenty-two plus twelve?
Well done for looking at how the numbers moved. When one goes up and the other goes down by the same, it balances.

Key words to use every time: balance, the same amount, give and take, blank. Do not teach 'compensation' or letters. Do not teach carrying. Totals are only used to check. Joining cold: every example can be shown with the two plates.
If a child writes the left total in the blank (8 plus 6 equals 7 plus 14): ask them to build both sides on the plates and say whether they match.
@rec

Stand up and get a sip of water. Arms out wide like a see-saw. Left hand shows some fingers, right hand shows some fingers. I say two numbers that make ten, and you show them. Then I say give one across.
Call 6 and 4, 5 and 5, 7 and 3. After each, say give one across and children move one finger to the other hand: still ten fingers. Then lean left, lean right, and sip water.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: fill in the missing numbers. Five plus three equals four plus blank. Six plus four equals five plus blank. Seven plus three equals blank plus seven. Two plus eight equals eight plus blank. Question 2: Mei puts 6 buttons and 2 buttons on the left plate. On the right plate she puts 7 buttons and some more. Draw the right plate. Question 3: Siti writes six plus three equals five plus nine. Is it balanced? Then fill in the missing number: six plus three equals five plus blank.

Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor looks around the gallery, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. Move to the answer slide only when most children have stopped writing; anyone not finished keeps going and checks later.

Answers for page 1. If you are still working, carry on and check later. Question 1: four, five, three, two. Question 2: one more button. Question 3: no, it is not balanced. The missing number is four.
Check your own page in another colour. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Everyone may choose, at any time.

Page 2. Question 4: seven plus five is twelve. Fill in the missing numbers: six plus blank equals twelve; five plus blank equals twelve; four plus blank equals twelve. Question 5: fill in the missing numbers. Twenty plus thirty equals forty plus blank. Fifty plus twenty equals sixty plus blank. Forty plus twenty equals thirty plus blank. Thirty plus thirty equals twenty plus blank. Question 6: Mei has 9 red pens and 6 blue pens. Ben has 10 red pens and some blue pens. They have the same number of pens. How many blue pens does Ben have? Question 7: thirty-five plus twelve equals blank plus two.
Page 2, questions 4 to 7. Move to the answer slide only when most children have stopped writing.
Answers for page 2. If you are still working, carry on and check later. Question 4: six, seven, eight. Question 5: ten, ten, thirty, forty. Question 6: Ben has five blue pens. Question 7: forty-five.
When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Everyone may choose. You can swap at any time.
Choice time: Think harder (page 3), Go further (page 4), the Investigation (page 5), or finish and check your own work. Tutor never says who is on which page.

Q2 (drawing): draw each pile as dots and make the right plate match the left. Q3: build 6 and 3 on one plate, then 5 and some more on the other. Q5 and Q7: ask did the first number go up or down, and by how much? Q6: how many pens does Mei have all together? Think harder T5: say the whole and the two parts. Two parts make the whole; take a part from the whole to find the other part.

A child who is still stuck ticks I am still stuck on their own look-back page. The grown-up may photograph that page and send it to the business WhatsApp after class. Open the next lesson with one short catch-up question for the whole group. Never a private message to a child, never a private room.

Think harder is for the idea taught today in a new setting: saying two sums are equal without adding. Go further is for mastery and extension. Do not announce who is on which page. Pairs are never split unless both children agree.
@rec
A child has 6 plus 4, which is 10. They add 1 to the 6 and 1 to the 4, and say 7 plus 5 is still 10. Do you agree? Use your plates to explain.
Build 6 and 4, then 7 and 5 on the plates. Is the total still the same?
Talk to the grown-up next to you or to your screen for one minute. Use the sentence starter: I think... because...
Who would like to share? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Remember puzzle two? Eight plus five equals nine plus a blank. Nine is one more than eight, so the blank is one less than five. The blank is four.
Did anyone change their mind about puzzle two while we worked? You can just nod.
Where did you use Act it out today?
Listen for the tool being named, not the answer. Volunteers first, a pass is always fine.

Model answer: No. 6 + 4 is 10 but 7 + 5 is 12. Ali added 1 to both numbers, so the total went up by 2. To keep 10, add 1 to one number and take 1 from the other: 7 + 3. Volunteers first; never call a child by name to answer; no tallies, no rankings. Praise the reason, not the speed.
@rec
Exit ticket. Three questions, on your own, without looking back. Write your answers on page 5. I will read them to you.

Question 1: fill in the missing number. Nine plus five equals ten plus blank. Question 2: is twenty-eight plus six equal to thirty plus four? Circle Yes or No. Question 3: fill in the missing number. Thirty plus twelve equals forty plus blank.
Children answer E1 to E3 on their own.
Four. Yes. Two: the thirty went up by ten, so the twelve goes down by ten.
If you made a mistake, that is useful. Put a dot by it and tell your grown-up what you will try next time.
Tick the ones you got right, in a different colour. Well done. Show your ticket to a grown-up.
Show me with your fingers how many you got right: three, two, one, or none yet. A pass is fine.

Look at the room as a whole, not at any one tile. If many children show one or two fingers, spend two minutes at the start of Lesson 9 on the two-sides idea, in the open session, no names. Do not write a child's name next to an answer and do not read out anyone's result.
@rec

Pick one problem from today. Did I answer the question? Does my answer make sense? Can I check it another way? Tick, write one word, or pass. If you tick I am still stuck, ask your grown-up to photograph this page after class and send it to our business WhatsApp. Then we will help you.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5. Nobody reads theirs out. Praise a check you saw, not speed.
@rec

Well done, inquirers. Next lesson is Draw and Measure. You need a ruler marked in centimetres, about ten paper clips, three or four small things to measure, a pencil and paper. If you have no ruler, tell your tutor before the lesson.
Optional, only if you are on time: twenty equals eleven plus a blank. And twenty equals twelve plus a blank. Keep going. What do you notice about the blanks?
Short think time, then take two answers.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

This is the standing buffer. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: 9, 8, 7, and so on; the first number goes up by one and the blank goes down by one. If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3b) instead of rushing on.
Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.

slides.title: Balance and Swap

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Balance two sides, and find missing numbers by giving and taking.

slides.note: Lesson 8 of Term 1, 90 minutes. Objective: understand the equals sign as balance and find a missing number by giving and taking between two numbers. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 28, mini-lesson 28 to 38, brain break 38 to 42, workbook 42 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Nobody is told which page they should be on. Remind the group that the lesson is recorded (the tutor, the screen and any voice that is not muted) and a child may keep the camera off.
slides.subtitle: Addition and subtraction: the equals sign

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: fingers to ten

blocks.text: I show 7. How many more fingers make 10?

slides.note: Say each number; children show on their fingers how many more make ten. Answers: 7 needs 3, 4 needs 6, 9 needs 1, 6 needs 4, 2 needs 8. This is a spiral review of the bonds to 10 (holiday topic) and lets a new child join: they hear it before they say it. No writing, no marks.

slides.title: Ten and more: how many to twenty?

blocks.text: Start at 13. How many more make 20?

slides.note: Answers: 13 needs 7, 16 needs 4, 18 needs 2, 15 needs 5. Say: look at the ones part. 3 needs 7 to make ten, so 13 needs 7 to make twenty. Show two full ten-frames if a child is unsure. This is the bonds to 20 idea the lesson uses when one number moves to the next ten.

slides.title: The equals sign

blocks.text: = means the same amount as
Is 3 + 4 the same amount as 6 + 2?

slides.note: Answers: 3 + 4 is the same amount as 5 + 2 (both 7). 3 + 4 is not the same amount as 6 + 2 (7 and 8). 4 + 4 is the same amount as 5 + 3 (both 8). Say clearly that the equals sign does not mean the answer comes next; it means the two sides are the same amount. Children answer with a thumb up or down.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Ravi has 6 red beads and 4 blue beads.
Siti has 5 red beads and 5 blue beads.
Do they have the same number of beads? Draw dots to help, then circle Yes or No.

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: What number goes in the blank? Write how you know.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 is an access question: any child can try it by drawing dots and counting. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson's key idea. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper up to the camera: children keep their own answer and check it at Talk time. No private chat and no board in front of the group. Answers: yes, 10 each; the blank is 4. Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list of who found it easy.

slides.title: Explore: two plates

items: Put your two plates side by side: LEFT and RIGHT.
Left plate: a pile of 6 and a pile of 4.
Right plate: a pile of 5, and a second pile.
Make the plates match. How many in the second pile?

blocks.head: WHAT IF?
items: What if the left plate has 7 and 3? What if it has 9 and 2?

slides.note: Round 1, about 5 minutes. Objects first, no writing yet. Children build the left plate, count it, then build the right plate so that it matches. Ask for a thumbs up when the plates match. Answers: 5 (6 + 4 = 5 + 5), then 2 (7 + 3 = 8 + 2), then 3 (9 + 2 = 8 + 3). The what-if card is available from the start so nobody waits, and no child is named for choosing it. A child with too few things can use the kit squares.

slides.title: Give and take

blocks.text: Left pile 7, right pile 5. Count all. Move 1 across. Count all again.
Next, match 8 + 4 with 9 + a second pile.

slides.note: Round 2 and round 3, about 8 minutes, main room. Children move one thing from one pile to the other and count the total again: it stays 12. Then give two or three across: 5 + 7 and 4 + 8 are still 12. Round 3 asks them to match 8 + 4 with 9 + a pile (3), and 6 + 5 with 8 + a pile (3), by thinking about how the first number moved. Look around the gallery and ask how do you know.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: When one number went up, what happened to the other?
Did the total change when we gave one across?
How could you find the second pile without counting everything?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key idea: when one number goes up, the other goes down by the same amount, and the total stays the same. We call it give and take. Repeat a child's answer in your own words so the recording picks it up.

slides.title: Equals means balance

blocks.text: 5 + 3 = 4 + 4. Both sides make 8.

slides.note: Show the two plates as a balanced see-saw. Both sides hold the same, so we write an equals sign between them. Ask: what does the equals sign mean? Answer: the two sides are the same amount. Say it is not a sign that the answer comes next.

slides.title: Give and take

rows: Take 1 from the 7, give it to the 5

blocks.text: The total stays the same.

slides.note: Think aloud: I take one from the seven, so seven becomes six. I give it to the five, so five becomes six. The total is still twelve. Ask: if I take one from the seven, what must I do to the five? Answer: give it one more. Link back to the Explore: this is what the plates showed.

slides.title: Your turn: the missing number

blocks.text: Write on your paper. About 2 minutes

slides.note: Each child writes on their own paper. Wait until most children have stopped writing. Do not ask children to hold boards up in front of the group. Joining cold: they may use the plates.

slides.title: Check: the missing number
slides.note: Answers: 7, 3, 7. Read each sentence aloud so a child watching the recording can mark their own work. The first number moved by 1 in the first two, and by 2 in the third: the blank moved the other way by the same amount.

slides.title: Bigger numbers, same idea

items: 25 went up to 27: 2 more.
So the blank is 2 less than 18.
The blank is 16.

slides.note: Worked example before the Start here page. Do not add first: look at how the number moved. 25 became 27, so 2 more. The other number must go down by 2: 18 becomes 16. Then check by adding both sides if the group is ready: both are 43. Ask: what number is two less than eighteen? Answer: sixteen.

slides.title: Same total? Do not add yet

cols.head: SAME TOTAL
items: 47 goes down 2. 18 goes up 2.

cols.head: NOT THE SAME
items: 29 goes up 1. 14 goes up 1.

blocks.text: One number goes down and one goes up by the same amount. The total stays the same.

slides.note: Worked example for Think harder. 47 to 45 is 2 less, and 18 to 20 is 2 more: the 2 moved across, so the totals are the same (65 each). 29 to 30 is 1 more and 14 to 15 is 1 more: both went up, so the total went up (43 and 45). Ask: same total or different, and how do you know? Keep to about two minutes; it is a worked example, not a skill to drill.

slides.title: Quick-fire: is it balanced?

blocks.text: Thumbs up: balanced. Thumbs down: not balanced.

slides.note: Answers: yes (6 up 1 to 7 and 5 down 1 to 4), no (8 up 1 to 9 but 3 stays the same, so the right side is 1 too big), yes (20 up 2 to 22 and 14 down 2 to 12). Children answer with thumbs; nobody writes. Ask how do you know after each one, and repeat a volunteer's reason in your own words.

slides.title: See-saw stand-up

blocks.text: Arms out wide like a see-saw. Left hand and right hand show the fingers.

items: 6 and 4
5 and 5
7 and 3

blocks.text: Give one across. Still ten fingers! Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera. Call each pair that makes ten and have children show it on their two hands; then say give one across and they move one finger from one hand to the other. Count the fingers: still ten. Lean left, lean right, sip water. Keep it gentle for small spaces.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. About 8 minutes

slides.note: Read questions 1 to 3 aloud with their numbers. Children work on their own; the tutor looks around the gallery and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children mark their own page in a different colour. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 7. About 9 minutes

slides.note: Read the questions aloud with their numbers. Question 6 is a story about pens: the children may draw the two sides. In question 7 the 12 became 2, which is one ten less: the other number goes up by one ten. Children may use the kit tens bars.

slides.title: Check page 2

start.text: Fill in the missing numbers. The balance shows part (a).
start.hint: Find the left side first. Then find what the right side needs. You can use your two plates.
mistakes: Writing the total of the left side in the blank (8 in part a).
Thinking the equals sign means the answer comes next.

start.text: Mei puts 6 buttons and 2 buttons on the left plate. On the right plate she puts 7 buttons and some more. Draw the buttons in the dashed box so both plates are the same.
start.hint: Count the left plate: 6 and 2. Then draw 7 dots on the right and add dots until it matches.
start.solution: The left plate has 6 + 2 = 8 buttons. The right plate has 7 buttons, so it needs 1 more to make 8.
mistakes: Drawing 8 more buttons on the right plate.
Forgetting the 7 buttons already there.

parts.text: Is it balanced? Circle Yes or No.

start.answer: No. The blank should be 4 (6 + 3 = 9 and 5 + 4 = 9). Siti wrote the total of the left side, as if = meant the answer comes next.
start.hint: Build 6 and 3 on your left plate. Then build 5 on the right plate. How many more make the plates match?
start.solution: 6 + 3 is 9. The right side must also be 9. 5 and 4 more make 9, so the blank is 4. Siti wrote 9, the total of the left side, but the blank is only one of the two numbers on the right.
mistakes: Saying yes because 9 is the answer to 6 + 3.
Writing 9 in the box again (copying Siti).

start.hint: The first number goes down by 1 each time, so the second number goes up by 1. You can use your plates.
start.solution: (a) 6 + 6 = 12. (b) 5 + 7 = 12. (c) 4 + 8 = 12. The first number goes down by 1 and the second goes up by 1, so the total stays 12.
mistakes: Leaving the second number as 5.
Making the second number go down as well.

start.hint: Did the first number go up or down? By how much? The other number does the opposite.
start.solution: (a) 20 went up by 20 to 40, so 30 goes down by 20 to 10. (b) 50 went up by 10 to 60, so 20 goes down by 10 to 10. (c) 40 went down by 10 to 30, so 20 goes up by 10 to 30. (d) 30 went down by 10 to 20, so 30 goes up by 10 to 40.
mistakes: Writing the total of the left side (50, 70, 60 or 60).
Moving both numbers the same way (part c: 20 - 10 = 10).

start.text: Mei has 9 red pens and 6 blue pens. Ben has 10 red pens and some blue pens. They have the same number of pens. How many blue pens does Ben have?
start.hint: Count Mei's pens first. Then see how many more Ben needs after his 10 red pens.
start.solution: Mei has 9 + 6 = 15 pens. Ben has 10 red pens, so he needs 5 more to make 15. Another way: his red pens are 1 more than Mei's, so his blue pens are 1 fewer: 5.
mistakes: Answering 6 (copying Mei's blue pens).
Answering 15 (the total).

start.hint: Add 35 + 12 first. Then think: what number and 2 make that total? Or move a tens bar from the 12 to the 35.
start.solution: The 12 went down by 10 to become 2, so the 35 goes up by 10 to become 45. Check: 35 + 12 = 47 and 45 + 2 = 47.
mistakes: Writing 47 (the total).
Writing 25 (taking a ten from the 35).

think.text: Mei says 56 + 17 and 54 + 19 have the same total. Ali says 54 + 19 has the greater total. Do not add.

parts.text: Who is right? Circle Mei or Ali.

think.answer: Mei. 56 went down by 2 to 54 and 17 went up by 2 to 19. The 2 moved across, so both totals are 73.
think.hint: Look at the first numbers: 56 and 54. Did it go up or down? By how much? What happened to 17 and 19?
think.solution: 56 to 54 is 2 less. 17 to 19 is 2 more. The 2 moved from one number to the other, so the total stays the same. Both sums make 73.
mistakes: Saying 54 + 19 is greater because 19 is a greater number than 17.
Adding both sums and not saying how the numbers moved (correct, but check the reason).

think.text: Do not add. Circle LEFT or RIGHT for the greater total, or circle SAME.
think.hint: For each pair ask: did the first number go up or down, and by how much? Did the second number do the opposite, by the same amount?
think.solution: (a) 29 up 1 to 30, 14 down 1 to 13: SAME (both 43). (b) 53 down 3 to 50, 20 up 3 to 23: SAME (both 73). (c) 26 up 2 to 28 and 15 up 1 to 16: both went up, so RIGHT is bigger (41 and 44).
mistakes: Saying SAME for part c because both numbers changed.
Looking only at the biggest numbers.

think.text: Fill in the missing number. Then find the total.
think.hint: 49 is 1 less than 50. Give that 1 to the 26 or take it from the 26? Then add 50 and the new number.
think.solution: 49 went up by 1 to 50, so 26 goes down by 1 to 25. 50 + 25 = 75, so 49 + 26 = 75.
mistakes: Writing 27 (making 26 go up as well).
Writing 75 in the blank.

parts.text: Is it balanced? Circle Yes or No.

think.answer: No. 24 + 17 = 41 but 26 + 19 = 45. Both numbers went up by 2. Change 19 to 15.
think.hint: Look at how 24 became 26, and how 17 became 19. Did the numbers move the same way, or opposite ways?
think.solution: 24 went up by 2 to 26, so 17 should go down by 2 to 15. Ben made it go up by 2 to 19, so the right side is 4 too big. Check: 24 + 17 = 41 and 26 + 15 = 41.
mistakes: Saying it is balanced because both numbers changed by 2.
Changing the 26 and not saying which number you change.

think.text: Use the three numbers 6, 9 and 15. The biggest number, 15, is the whole. Fill in the number sentences.

parts.text: Ali writes 9 - 6 = 15. Is it true? Circle Yes or No.

think.answer: 15, 6, 9, 9, No (9 - 6 = 3; the whole, 15, goes first in a take-away)
think.hint: Two small numbers make the big one: 6 and 9 make 15. To take away, start at the big number, 15.
think.solution: 6 + 9 = 15. 9 + 6 = 15, so the blank in (b) is 6. Taking one part from the whole leaves the other part: 15 - 6 = 9 and 15 - 9 = 6, so the blank in (d) is 9. Ali is not right: 9 - 6 = 3, not 15. The whole, 15, is the number you start from when you take away.
mistakes: Writing 9 in (b) because 9 is in the line.
Writing 6 in (d) because 6 is on the right.
Saying Yes to (e) because the same three numbers are used.

go.text: Fill in the missing numbers so that all three sums have the same total.
go.hint: Find the first blank by giving and taking: 19 went up by 1. Then 20 + 27 = 47 is the total. What goes with 30?
go.solution: 19 up 1 to 20, so 28 down 1 to 27. The total is 20 + 27 = 47 (check: 19 + 28 = 47). Then [] + 30 = 47, so the second blank is 47 - 30 = 17.
mistakes: Writing 27 in both blanks.
Writing 30 or 28 as the second blank.

go.text: Fill in the blanks so both sides are the same. Write 3 different pairs. Many answers are right.
go.answer: Any pair where the first blank is 4 more than the second, for example 5 and 1, 6 and 2, 7 and 3 (also 4 and 0).
go.hint: Try a small number for the second blank, for example 1. What does the first blank need to be?
go.solution: If the second blank is 1, the right side is 10, so the first blank is 5. If it is 2, the right side is 11, so the first blank is 6. The first blank is always 4 more than the second, because 9 is 4 more than 5.
mistakes: Writing the same number in both blanks.
Giving one pair only.

go.text: Mei has 28 stickers on a page and 17 in her pocket. Ali, Ben and Kumar have the same total as Mei. Fill in the blanks.

parts.text: Ali has 30 stickers on his page. His pocket has [] stickers.
Ben has 25 stickers on his page. His pocket has [] stickers.
Kumar has 12 stickers in his pocket. His page has [] stickers.

go.hint: Ali's page has 2 more than Mei's page. So his pocket has 2 fewer. Ben's page has 3 fewer than Mei's page. For Kumar, his pocket has 5 fewer than Mei's, so his page has 5 more.
go.solution: Mei has 28 + 17 = 45. Ali: 30 is 2 more than 28, so his pocket has 2 fewer than 17: 15. Ben: 25 is 3 fewer than 28, so his pocket has 3 more than 17: 20. Kumar: his pocket 12 is 5 fewer than 17, so his page has 5 more than 28: 33. Check: 30 + 15 = 45, 25 + 20 = 45 and 33 + 12 = 45.
mistakes: Writing 17 for Ali's pocket.
Making Ben's pocket 14 (moving the wrong way).
Writing 17 or 45 for Kumar's page.

investigation.title: Keep it the same
investigation.first: Add 6 + 4, then 7 + 3, then 7 + 5. Which total is not 10? Then look at 6 + 4 and 7 + 3: the 6 goes up 1. What does the 4 do?
investigation.text: Pick two numbers. Add 3 to one and take 3 from the other. Then add 3 to both. Then take 2 from both. Which keep the total the same? By how much do the others change it?
investigation.answer: First step: 7 + 5 is not 10 (the totals are 10, 10 and 12). From 6 + 4 to 7 + 3 the 4 goes down 1. Next: add some to one number and take the same from the other and the total stays the same (give and take). Add 3 to both: the total goes up by 6. Take 2 from both: the total goes down by 4. When both numbers change the same way, the total changes by double.
val: first step: 7 + 5 is not 10; the 4 goes down 1
same when one up and one down by the same
investigation.look_for: A child who tries more than one pair of numbers, says it stays the same when one goes up and the other goes down by the same amount, and notices that changing both numbers the same way changes the total by double. Any clear reason is fine.
mistakes: Saying adding the same to both numbers keeps the total the same (the total goes up by double).
Testing only one pair of numbers.

talk.question: Ali has 6 + 4, which is 10. He adds 1 to the 6 and adds 1 to the 4. He says 7 + 5 is still 10. Do you agree? Use your plates to explain.
talk.answer: No. 6 + 4 is 10 but 7 + 5 is 12. Ali made both numbers bigger, so the total went up by 2. To keep 10, add 1 to one number and take 1 from the other: 7 + 3.
talk.look_for: A reason that says one number must go up while the other goes down (not just 'because 12 is not 10').

exit.solution: 9 went up by 1 to 10, so 5 goes down by 1 to 4. Both sides make 14.
mistakes: Writing 14 (the total).
Writing 6 (making the 5 go up).

exit.solution: 28 went up by 2 to 30 and 6 went down by 2 to 4. Both sides make 34.
mistakes: Writing no because the numbers look different.

exit.answer: 2. The 30 went up by 10 to 40, so the 12 goes down by 10 to 2.
exit.solution: 30 went up by 10, so 12 goes down by 10 to 2. Both sides make 42.
mistakes: Writing 42 (the total).
Writing 22 (making the 12 go up).

home_practice.solution: 6 + 3 is 9, and 5 + 4 is 9. The 6 became 5 (1 less), so the 3 becomes 4 (1 more).
10 went down by 1 to 9, so 4 goes up by 1 to 5. Both sides make 14.
20 went up by 20 to 40, so 30 goes down by 20 to 10. Both sides make 50.

home_practice.text: Ravi says 36 + 14 and 34 + 16 have the same total. Do not add. Is he right? Circle Yes or No. Then write: I know because ___.
home_practice.answer: Yes. 36 went down by 2 to 34 and 14 went up by 2 to 16. Both make 50.
home_practice.solution: One number goes down by 2 and the other goes up by 2, so the total stays the same.

home_practice.text: Put 12 small things in a pile of 7 and a pile of 5. Give 1 across and write the new sum, like 6 + 6 = 12. Write all the sums you can find. Many answers are right.
home_practice.answer: Any list that shows the first number going down by 1 and the second going up by 1, for example 7 + 5, 6 + 6, 5 + 7, 4 + 8, 3 + 9, 2 + 10, 1 + 11, 0 + 12.
home_practice.solution: Each time one thing moves across, the total stays 12. A grown-up can count the things on both piles to check.

online_practice.title: Balance and Swap
online_practice.topic: The equals sign and giving and taking

items.q: Fill in the missing number so both sides are the same: 5 + 3 = 4 + ___
items.hint: The 5 became 4. It went down by 1. So what happens to the 3?

slips.say: 8 is the total of 5 + 3. The blank is only one of the two numbers on the right side.

tpl.q: Fill in the missing number so both sides are the same: {a} + {b} = {c} + ___
tpl.hint: The {a} became {c}. It went down by {k}. So what happens to the {b}?

items.q: Fill in the missing number so both sides are the same: 4 + 7 = 6 + ___
items.hint: The 4 became 6. It went up by 2. So what happens to the 7?

slips.say: 11 is the total of 4 + 7. The blank is one of the numbers on the right side.

tpl.q: Fill in the missing number so both sides are the same: {a} + {b} = {c} + ___
tpl.hint: The {a} became {c}. It went up by {k}. So what happens to the {b}?

items.q: Which sum is the same amount as 6 + 4?
steps: The 6 went down by 1 and the 4 went up by 1.

slips.say: 5 + 4 makes 9. 6 + 4 makes 10. Add both sides first.

items.hint: 30 went up by 10 to 40. What happens to the other 30?
steps: So the other 30 goes down by 10.

slips.say: 60 is the total of 30 + 30. The blank is one of the two numbers on the right.

tpl.hint: {a} went up by 10 to {c}. What happens to the {b}?

items.q: Siti fills in 8 + 6 = 9 + ___. Which number goes in the blank?
items.hint: 8 + 6 makes 14. The right side must make 14 too. What goes with 9?
steps: The right side must make 14 too.
9 and 5 make 14, so the blank is 5.

slips.say: 14 is the total of the left side. The right side is 9 plus the blank, and that must also make 14.

items.hint: 49 went up by 1 to 50. What happens to the 26?

slips.say: 75 is the total. The blank is the number that goes with 50.
27 is 1 more than 26. The 49 went up, so 26 must go down.

tpl.hint: {a} went up by {y} to {c}. What happens to the {b}?

items.q: Do not add. Which sum has the same total as 47 + 18?
items.hint: 47 became a different number. Did the 18 move the opposite way by the same amount?

slips.say: Both numbers went down. One must go down and the other must go up.

items.q: Do not add. Which total is greater: 29 + 14 or 30 + 15?
items.hint: Did the numbers move the same way or opposite ways?
steps: Both went up, so 30 + 15 is greater.

slips.say: Both numbers went up by 1. That makes the total 2 greater.

items.q: Ben wrote 24 + 17 = 26 + 19. It is not balanced. What number should replace the 19?
items.hint: Look at how the first number moved. The other number must move the opposite way.
steps: So 17 must go down by 2, not up.

slips.say: 19 is what Ben wrote. Both numbers went up by 2, so the total is too big.

tpl.q: Ben wrote {a} + {b} = {c} + {d}. It is not balanced. What number should replace the {d}?
tpl.hint: {a} went up by {k} to {c}. The other number must move the opposite way.
steps: So {b} must go down by {k}, not up.

items.q: Fill in both blanks: 19 + 28 = 20 + ___ = ___ + 30. There are two blanks. Type both numbers in order, with a comma between them.
items.hint: Find the first blank by giving and taking. Then find the total, and the second blank.
steps: 19 went up by 1 to 20, so 28 goes down by 1 to 27.
47 take away 30 is 17. The blanks are 27 and 17.

items.q: Mei has 28 stickers on a page and 17 in her pocket. Ali has the same total as Mei. He has 30 on a page. How many are in his pocket?
items.hint: Compare Ali's page with Mei's page. Does his pocket have more or fewer?
steps: Ali's page has 2 more than Mei's.
So his pocket has 2 fewer than 17.

slips.say: 17 is Mei's pocket. Ali has more on his page, so fewer in his pocket.

tpl.q: Mei has {a} stickers on a page and {b} in her pocket. Ali has the same total as Mei. He has {c} on a page. How many are in his pocket?
tpl.hint: Compare Ali's page with Mei's page. Does his pocket have more or fewer?
steps: Ali's page has {k} more than Mei's.
So his pocket has {k} fewer than {b}.

items.q: ___ + 5 = 9 + ___. The first blank is how many more than the second blank?
items.hint: Try a small number for the second blank. What must the first blank be?
steps: Try the second blank as 1: the right side is 10.
The first blank must be 5, which is 4 more than 1.
The first blank is always 4 more.

slips.say: 9 is on the right side already. Try numbers in the blanks and see how far apart they are.

tpl.q: ___ + {p} = {q} + ___. The first blank is how many more than the second blank?
tpl.hint: Try a small number for the second blank. What must the first blank be?
steps: Try the second blank as 1: the right side is {q} + 1.
The first blank plus {p} must match it.
The first blank is always {ans} more.

items.q: Make up your own puzzle like 27 + 14 = 30 + ___. Check it by adding both sides.
items.hint: Pick a sum first. Change one number, then find the blank.
steps: Pick two numbers to add, for example 27 and 14.
Change the first number, for example to 30. It went up by 3.
The blank is 3 less than 14: it is 11. Check: 27 + 14 = 41 and 30 + 11 = 41.

parent.summary: We learned that the equals sign means 'the same amount as', like a balanced see-saw. Your child balanced two plates of small things and found missing numbers like 6 + 3 = 5 + ___. Give and take: when one number goes up, the other goes down by the same amount. Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose, so some sums have tens; we explore them with objects first. Each week we suggest Home Practice (about 15 minutes); pages 3 to 5 and online practice are optional.
words: equals (=): the two sides are the same amount
balance: both sides hold the same
give and take: add some to one number and take the same from the other
blank: the line where the missing number goes
try_home: Two plates: put a pile of buttons on each plate (7 on the left, 5 on the right). Ask: are they the same? Move one across and count again.
Say it: write 8 + 5 = 9 + ___ and ask your child to say how the 8 moved and what that means for the 5.
Make a mistake on purpose: write 7 + 3 = 8 + 3 and ask your child to find what is wrong and fix it.
ask: Did the first number go up or down?
What must the other number do?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child use two plates and small things or draw the two sides, and wait 10 seconds before helping. Please do not teach the column method yet, and do not hurry. If your child ticked I am still stuck on the look-back page, photograph that page and send it to the business WhatsApp, +65 9880 5962, after class. Photos are kept for 90 days after the program ends, then deleted.
parent.next: Lesson 9: Draw and Measure. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted; your child may mute and keep the camera off. The recording link is private to your family: please do not share it.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones and to say why. This week: the equals sign as balance, and finding a missing number by giving and taking.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to see numbers as tens and ones, to notice patterns and to say why.
parent.quote: Adjust one side, adjust the other. When one number goes up, the other goes down by the same amount.
next_materials: A ruler marked in cm, starting at 0. No ruler? Tell your tutor now; we will help
10 paper clips (or small same-size things) and 3 or 4 things to measure
The printed Lesson 9 workbook (print at 100%, actual size), a pencil and spare paper

safeguarding: Small things stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper or work up to the camera: a gallery view shows everyone. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on three, or show fingers or a thumb for a choice. There is no private chat and no board held up in front of the group.

Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. The recording captures the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. Never show a child's page on the recording.

A child who needs help ticks I am still stuck on their own look-back page. The grown-up may photograph that page and send it to the program's business WhatsApp after class (never to a personal phone); the tutor replies to the grown-up only. The next lesson starts with one short catch-up question for the whole group. No private messages to children and no private room.
Movement break: children need a little clear space, soft shoes or socks on a safe floor, no stairs and no running. A child may stay seated and move only their arms.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first, and try the two-plates routine with real things.

Tell parents a week before: print workbook pages 1 to 6, cut out the kit page (page 6), find about 30 small things of one kind and two plates or bowls. Lesson 9 needs a centimetre ruler: ask families who have none to tell the tutor.
Have the slides open. To show your two plates to the recording, use a shared whiteboard or a blank slide; the recording does not show your webcam tile.

Test the recording once with several tiles before the first live class: check that it captures the tutor, the shared screen and any unmuted voice, and not the children's faces. Write the setting you used in your tutor notes.

Say plainly if a parent asks: Term 1 goes beyond the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose. Every Start here item is built to be reached with bars, bundles or a number line and a worked step, and the program does not claim to match any school syllabus. Items that need more than that sit at Think harder.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content. If you are more than 3 minutes ahead at minute 42, use one menu activity then.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask 'How do you know?' and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: you can swap the two numbers in an addition and the total stays the same. Try 8 + 5 and 5 + 8, then 12 + 7 and 7 + 12, with your plates. Is it always true? What about taking away: 9 - 4 and 4 - 9?
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Try 8 + 5 and 5 + 8 with your plates. Is swapping always true? Try 9 - 4 and 4 - 9.
menu.answer: For adding, yes: the two piles just change places, so the total is the same. For taking away, no: 9 take away 4 is 5, but you cannot take 9 from 4.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Pick a sum like 14 + 6. Change the first number and leave a blank for the second, like 16 + ___. Give it to your grown-up to fill in so that it balances.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Write a missing-number puzzle like 16 + ___ = 14 + 6 for a grown-up to solve.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check by adding both sides: for example 14 + 6 = 20 and 16 + 4 = 20, so the blank is 4.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never seen a blank. Teach them how to find the blank in 25 + 18 = 27 + ___ without adding first.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how to find the blank in 25 + 18 = 27 + ___ without adding first.
menu.answer: 27 is 2 more than 25, so the blank is 2 less than 18. The blank is 16.

workbook.home_hint: Use two plates and small things, or draw both sides.

kits.title: Kit page: tens bars and ones squares
kits.intro: A grown-up cuts these out before the lesson. A bar is a ten. A square is a one. They help with questions S5 and S7 (the tens). For the two plates, use real plates. Keep the pieces in an envelope.
